cf.title: Use a hash table for the regexp cache

input.subject: Use a hash table for the regexp cache

verdict_reasoning: No surviving objection finds a flaw in the design of 0001. Both surviving objections are about demand and timing. With the limit kept at 32, message #1 shows gains only up to 32 patterns and no change at 33 or more (maintenance-fit-1). The thread cites no workload that uses more than 32 patterns per backend (demand-1). The list should agree on the sizing direction before 0001 is reviewed as groundwork.

brief.title: Use a hash table for the per-backend regexp cache
brief.problem: Each backend caches at most 32 compiled regexps (MAX_CACHED_RES, fixed at compile time) in an array searched linearly. Workloads that cycle through more than 32 patterns recompile on every call, about 9x slower in the author's benchmark. The linear search also removes the gain from a larger limit, because a hit in a 1000-entry array costs about as much as compiling.
brief.proposed_design: v1-0001 replaces the array with a simplehash table keyed by pattern, flags and collation, plus a dlist in LRU order, so lookup and move-to-front are O(1). The most recently used entry is compared before hashing, and each cached_re_str lives in its regexp's own memory context so the returned regex_t no longer moves. The limit stays at 32; a sizing GUC is left for a later patch.
user_visible_surface: RE_compile_and_cache() in regex/regex.h: the returned regex_t now stays at a stable address while the cache is reorganized.
author_claims: Behavior is unchanged: same limit of 32 and same move-to-front policy.
No regression for a single repeated pattern (2.79 ms vs 2.84 ms) and about 11% faster at 32 patterns.
With MAX_CACHED_RES=1024, a 1000-pattern workload is about 7.5 times faster than the array at the same limit.
An ERROR during compile or insert leaves the cache consistent.
A query-lifetime cache in fn_extra would be about 30% slower per short query and cannot cover SRFs, jsonpath, the planner or extensions.
brief.thread_state: jian he proposed a query-level cache in fn_extra instead of the session cache; the author replied with measurements and caller cases against it. No one has reviewed the patch itself or answered the sizing question (memory GUC, count GUC, or a higher compiled-in limit).
unclear: The patch does not say whether a larger hash table costs more per backend than the array when few patterns are used.
No benchmark shows the gain at the current limit of 32 matters for real workloads, since the 33+ cases are unchanged.
The thread does not say which sizing option the author will pursue if no one answers, or whether 0001 is worth committing without it.
The benchmark covers one platform and one client only.

objections.title: Groundwork commit has little value until the sizing question is settled
objections.failure_scenario: A committer pushes 0001, which replaces a short array loop with a simplehash table plus a dlist. If the list never agrees on a sizing option, users with 33 or more patterns still recompile on every call. The project then maintains more complex cache code for about 11% at exactly 32 patterns.
objections.argument: With the default limit, message #1 shows gains only up to 32 patterns, and the 33, 64 and 1024 rows are unchanged. The large gains appear only with MAX_CACHED_RES=1024, which the patch does not ship. The commit message calls 0001 "groundwork", and message #1 leaves the next step open among three options with no reply yet. A committer would likely ask to see the sizing direction agreed, or posted as 0002, before taking on the extra structure.
objections.author_must_show: Which sizing option will follow, and if none is agreed, does 0001 alone help a real workload enough to justify the more complex cache?

critic.reasoning: Message #1's default-limit table shows no change at 33 or more patterns, and the commit message calls 0001 groundwork. simplehash and dlist are existing infrastructure, which lowers the cost, but no one has answered the sizing question.

objections.title: No workload shown that cycles through more than 32 regexps
objections.failure_scenario: A committer merges the new cache structure and then adds a sizing GUC. No user turns out to run more than 32 distinct patterns per backend, so every backend carries extra code and one more setting that nobody tunes.
objections.argument: The only evidence of demand is a wiki TODO entry and a 2008 thread (message #1). No field report, -general or -bugs thread, or production workload is cited for the 33+ case, which is the case where the 9x cost appears. The benchmark is synthetic: each query cycles through N patterns on purpose. Message #2 questions the session-level design itself, and nobody in the thread reports needing a larger cache.
objections.author_must_show: Which real applications or reports show backends regularly using more than 32 distinct regexps, and what recompile cost do they measure today?

critic.reasoning: The TODO entry and the 2008 thread show the interest has lasted, but the thread cites no workload that uses more than 32 patterns. The sizing GUC in the failure scenario is not part of 0001 and should not count against it.

refuted.title: 0001 alone gives little benefit while the next step is undecided
refuted.failure_scenario: 0001 is committed as groundwork, but the sizing question gets no agreement and the follow-up never lands. The cache code is then more complex, with a hash table, a dlist and changed ownership of the pattern string, and in the author's own table the gain is about 11% at 32 patterns and nothing for 33 or more.
refuted.argument: Message #1 says 0001 keeps the limit at 32 and that its purpose is to make a larger limit useful. With the default limit, the measured changes run from 2% slower to 11% faster, and they come from one machine and one client. Message #1 also notes that a larger cache could cost about 13 MB per backend, so the payoff depends on a sizing decision that has not been discussed.
refuted.author_must_show: Is 0001 worth committing if the cache limit stays at 32, and which sizing option will follow it?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of maintenance-fit-1, which makes the same point with a more concrete request (agree the sizing direction or post it as 0002).

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: RE_compile_and_cache() is exported in regex/regex.h, and the regex_t it returns now stays at a stable address.

touch_points.label: new GUC
touch_points.reason: 0001 adds no GUC, but message #1 proposes a sizing GUC (by memory or by count) as the next step.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: A simplehash table plus a dlist replaces a short array loop in regexp.c.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: Every regexp operator and function call goes through the cache lookup that the patch rewrites.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)
touch_points.reason: see objection demand-1: No workload shown that cycles through more than 32 regexps

questions: Which sizing option (memory GUC, count GUC, or a higher compiled-in limit) will follow 0001, and can it be posted as 0002 in the same series?
Which real applications or reports show backends that regularly use more than 32 distinct regexps, and what recompile cost do they measure today?
If the limit stays at 32, does 0001 alone help a real workload enough to justify the more complex cache?
How much memory per backend does the hash table use compared with the array when only a few patterns are cached?
Do the benchmark results hold on a second platform and with more than one client?

committability.owner_note: Someone who knows the regex code in regexp.c and backend memory contexts would have to own it. No committer has spoken in the visible thread.
committability.liability: The owner signs for cache consistency after an ERROR and for the lifetime of the regex_t returned to callers, including extensions, for as long as the cache exists.
committability.author_follow_up: The author answered message #2 within a day with measurements, offered to prototype the alternative, and said they will follow cfbot results.

not_now.evidence_that_would_change_it: A field report or production workload where backends cycle through more than 32 distinct regexps, with the recompile cost measured. Agreement on one sizing option, or a 0002 patch that implements it, would also change the answer.

priority.reason: The patch is about 16 KiB, local to regexp.c, and uses existing simplehash and dlist code. With the limit at 32 it gains about 11% at best, so it belongs in one series with the sizing patch that gives it its value.

provisional_note: Without the code, the claim that an ERROR during compile or insert leaves the cache consistent could not be checked. The same holds for whether a caller's regex_t stays valid when its entry is evicted.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: change regexp_substr first argument make tests more easier to understand
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch changes the input string in the regexp_substr() regression tests in strings.sql from 'abcabcabc' to 'abcaXcaYc', so each match returns a different substring. A later version also changed the regexp_instr() tests the same way.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane argued that these tests exist to show the functions' behavior with several copies of the target substring. With distinct substrings, a correct result could also come from the pattern failing to match elsewhere, so the change weakens the tests. Tomas Vondra had earlier asked whether the change made the tests weaker. The entry was then withdrawn.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Thus, what Jian is proposing breaks the
tests: it's no longer perfectly clear whether the result is because
the function did what we expect, or because the pattern failed to
match anywhere else.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add regexp_positions(string text, pattern text, flags text) → setof record (starts integer[], lengths integer[])
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add a regexp_positions() function that works like regexp_matches() but returns the positions of matches and capture groups instead of the matched substrings. An earlier int4range[] return type was dropped because empty ranges cannot represent zero-length matches, and the later version returned setof record with parallel arrays of start positions and lengths.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane reviewed the revised patch and raised definitional questions that were still open: whether to add a search-start-position argument, the need for a regexp_match()-style single-result variant, whether separate start and length arrays are confusing, and how sub-matches should be handled. He also listed code and documentation problems. The author did not respond to this review for two months, so the entry was returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I am on board now with the general
idea of returning match positions, but I think there are still
definitional issues to be discussed.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Auto-tune effective_cache size to be 4x shared buffers"
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Auto-tune effective_cache size to be 4x shared buffers"
Reverted commit(s): Auto-tune effective_cache size to be 4x shared buffers
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit ee1e5662d8d8330726eaef7d3110cb7add24d058, as well as
a remarkably large number of followup commits, which were mostly concerned
with the fact that the implementation didn't work terribly well.  It still
doesn't: we probably need some rather basic work in the GUC infrastructure
if we want to fully support GUCs whose default varies depending on the
value of another GUC.  Meanwhile, it also emerged that there wasn't really
consensus in favor of the definition the patch tried to implement (ie,
effective_cache_size should default to 4 times shared_buffers).  So whack
it all back to where it was.  In a followup commit, I'll do what was
recently agreed to, which is to simply change the default to a higher
value.

precedents_retrieved.title: WIP: Track relation size in shared memory
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a pool of SMgrSharedRelation objects in shared memory that holds the authoritative size of each recently extended or truncated relation until the file is fsync'd, so backends stop calling lseek(SEEK_END). The aim was fewer system calls and correct sizes on filesystems such as NFS that can shrink files asynchronously; an earlier recovery-only size cache from the same thread was committed separately (c5315f4f).
precedents_retrieved.objection: The patch stayed at prototype stage. The author said a main piece was missing: a background process to clean dirty SR objects, so that foreground processes rarely block on fsync during eviction. Review comments from Buzhen, Andres and later Anastasia Lubennikova were still open, for example on CREATE DATABASE, which bypasses smgr, and on temporary relations. The visible messages show no reply after the July 2021 review before the entry was closed.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: The main thing being: how can we clean these objects in the background?  That question being unanswered, there is a 0% chance of committing this in PostgreSQL 14.

precedents_retrieved.title: XLog size reductions: Reduced XLog record header size
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patchset makes the WAL record header variable-length, which shrinks it to 14-21 bytes, with about 4-5% less WAL estimated for pgbench. It varlength-encodes the record length, gives rmgrs their own info byte, includes the XID only when the record asks for it with XLOG_INCLUDE_XID, and adds an invalid rmgr ID 0 used to detect the end of WAL.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author stopped responding after review. Michael Paquier objected to the opt-in XLOG_INCLUDE_XID interface and questioned the use of rmgr ID 0 as an end-of-WAL marker. Pavel Borisov then asked for benchmarks showing the gain was large enough, the benchmarking was still a todo, and a reminder from Andrey M. Borodin in April 2024 got no visible reply before the entry was returned.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
But at the second round, some doubt arises on whether this long
patchset indeed introduces enough performance gain?

precedents_retrieved.title: guc-ify the formerly hard-coded MAX_SEND_SIZE to max_wal_send
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch turns the hard-coded MAX_SEND_SIZE of 128 KiB, the most data walsender sends at once, into a GUC max_wal_send with an upper bound of XLOG_SEG_SIZE (16 MiB by default). The author reported about 2x better replication throughput in a lab test over high bandwidth-delay links.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author could not reproduce the earlier throughput gain in new tests, and a test machine failed. Reviewers had asked why the OS network stack would not already handle this. The patch also lacked documentation in config.sgml and had a wrong lower bound, so David Steele returned it to give the author time to test and refine it.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
My recommendation is that we mark this patch "Returned with Feedback" to
allow you time to test and refine the patch.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Add single-item cache when looking at topmost XID of a subtrans XID"
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Add single-item cache when looking at topmost XID of a subtrans XID"
Reverted commit(s): Add single-item cache when looking at topmost XID of a subtrans XID
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit 06f5295 as per issues with this approach, both in
terms of efficiency impact and stability.  First, contrary to the
single-item cache for transaction IDs in transam.c, the cache may finish
by not be hit for a long time, and without an invalidation mechanism to
clear it, it would cause inconsistent results on wraparound for
example.  Second, the use of SubTransGetTopmostTransaction() for the
caching has a limited impact on performance.  SubTransGetParent() could
have more impact, though the benchmarking of the single-item approach
still needs to be proved, particularly under the conditions where SLRU
lookups are stressed in parallel with overflowed snapshots (aka more
than 64 subxids generated, for example).

After discussion with Andres Freund.

precedents_retrieved.title: Support regular expressions with nondeterministic collations
precedents_retrieved.summary: Allow regular expression functions and operators with nondeterministic collations by ignoring the collate part of the collation and keeping only its ctype behaviour. SIMILAR TO patterns, which the SQL standard defines in terms of the collation, get an internal "***S" prefix so they still raise an error under a nondeterministic collation.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected that the patch adds no functionality and forecloses a later, collation-aware definition, and he asked to first check whether the SQL committee knew how to implement its SIMILAR TO definition. The committee had no consensus on the right semantics. Discussion then turned to case-folding approaches for case-insensitive collations, and Peter Eisentraut withdrew the patch in favour of special-purpose collations such as "normal but case insensitive".
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
It adds no
functionality, and it forecloses the possibility of changing
the definition later.

precedents_retrieved.title: replace magic num in struct cachedesc with CATCACHE_MAXKEYS
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch replaces the literal array size 4 in the key field of struct cachedesc in syscache.c with CATCACHE_MAXKEYS. CatCache and CatCTup already use that constant.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Peter Eisentraut said that syscache and catcache are formally separate, so the syscache limit of 4 keys is not necessarily the same value as CATCACHE_MAXKEYS. The author accepted this and withdrew the entry.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
So I don't think the "4" in the
syscache is necessarily the same as CATCACHE_MAXKEYS.

precedents_retrieved.title: JIT compilation per plan node
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch moves the JIT compilation decision from the whole query to each plan node, so a node is compiled when its cost times its estimated number of calls exceeds jit_above_cost. Inlining and optimization stay decided per query, and the patch passes estimated calls through createplan.c with a new CreatePlanContext.
precedents_retrieved.objection: No visible message states why the entry was withdrawn. Tomas Vondra and Robert Haas supported moving the decision to the node level. In the last messages, David Rowley questioned plan node total cost as the measure, proposed using the estimated number of executions of each ExprState instead, and said the costing design was still undecided. The thread then stops, three months before the withdrawal.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Anyway, I don't think it's worth talking in detail about specifics about implementation for the total cost of the node idea when the whole replacement costing model design is still undecided.

roaster_notes.note: None of the listed precedents is this idea. [P8] reverted a subtrans XID cache for invalidation and wraparound reasons that do not apply to a regexp cache. [P7] and [P14] made a constant into a GUC, which 0001 does not do. The 2008 discussion cited in message #1 raised three concerns: measuring regexps in bytes, a dedicated count GUC, and O(N) search beyond about 1000 entries. Message #1 reports the first is gone and 0001 addresses the third. The GUC question is left for a later patch, so no earlier rejection reason applies to 0001.

From the standards and compatibility angle, 0001 changes no SQL syntax, GUC, catalog, dump output or psql behaviour, and it keeps the same limit of 32 and the same move-to-front eviction. The only contract change is that RE_compile_and_cache() now returns a regex_t at a stable address, which weakens a constraint on callers and breaks none. The sizing GUC (memory or count) would need this review when it is proposed, but it is not part of this patch.

The patch only changes a per-backend, in-memory cache in regexp.c, so it touches no persistent or cross-node state: no on-disk format, WAL, catalog, protocol or replication change. RE_compile_and_cache() keeps its signature, and its result now stays at one address, which only strengthens what extensions get; whether the internal struct is visible outside regexp.c could not be checked without the code.

v1-0001 changes only the private lookup structure of a per-backend cache: same 32-entry limit, same key (pattern, flags, collation), no new privilege, view or shared state. The entry cap keeps hash collisions from user-chosen patterns small, and per-backend memory does not grow. A later sizing GUC would need its own review of the default and of who may raise it.

Only one objection from this angle. The change is local to regexp.c, uses existing simplehash and dlist infrastructure, adds no GUC or catalog state, and keeps the single-pattern path to one comparison.

Postgres has no other way to get this result: MAX_CACHED_RES is a compile-time constant, and raising it makes lookups slow because the search is linear. No extension or hook can replace the backend regexp cache, and the patch reuses simplehash and dlist. The query-level fn_extra cache from message #2 was answered in message #3 with measurements and with callers that have no usable fn_extra.
The precedents listed concern walsender and subtransaction caches and do not apply to the demand question here.
